name: Testosterone gel (AndroGel)

lead: Testosterone gel is a prescription gel applied to the skin to treat low testosterone in men; AndroGel is the best-known brand. Its appearance interest comes from muscle and body composition: leaner, more muscular physiques once levels are restored.

The chain: testosterone is absorbed through the skin, circulating levels rise, and lean mass tends to go up while fat mass goes down. Studies in hypogonadal men report normalised testosterone and improvements in sexual function, mood, lean mass and bone density. Cosmetic use in men with normal levels is off-label and less studied.

paras: It is used as a daily gel under a prescriber's direction, often by men who want a steady alternative to injections. Lab monitoring is part of routine care, and body-composition changes in trials build over months.

Reported effects include acne, breast enlargement, raised hematocrit and sperm suppression, with cardiovascular and clot concerns discussed for testosterone products. Skin contact can transfer it to women and children, and virilisation has occurred in exposed people. It is a controlled substance needing a prescription in most countries.

angle.text: Testosterone gel is prescribed for diagnosed low testosterone, and users discuss it as a TRT option for muscle, body composition and energy. Trials in hypogonadal men show gains in lean mass and drops in fat mass; use for looks in men with normal levels is off-label.

lead: Testosterone gel is a prescription topical form of testosterone replacement therapy applied to the skin, sold under brand names including AndroGel, Testim, TestoGel and Fortesta.[1] It is prescribed mainly for male hypogonadism, in which the body produces too little testosterone, and is also used in masculinising hormone therapy for transgender men.[1]

In a 2004 study of 163 hypogonadal men followed for up to 42 months, continuous gel use normalised average serum testosterone levels.[2] In muscle and appearance-focused communities the gel is discussed as a steadier alternative to injections, usually in the context of testosterone replacement therapy rather than as a cosmetic product. Wikipedia notes that the US FDA stated in 2015 that benefits and safety of testosterone for age-related low testosterone had not been established.[1]
infobox: Testosterone first approved for medical use
Rx-only; US Schedule III, Canada Schedule IV, UK Class C

paras: The primary indication is testosterone replacement in men with hypogonadism, with transgender masculinising therapy as a further use.[1] Wikipedia reports AndroGel as the most popular testosterone form for hypogonadism in the United States, and a 2020 American College of Physicians guideline suggested intramuscular rather than transdermal treatment on the basis of similar effectiveness and harms with lower cost.[1]

Interest in appearance centres on muscle, fat distribution and energy. The 2004 long-term study of AndroGel in hypogonadal men reported benefits on sexual function, mood, lean and fat mass and bone mineral density.[2] Those findings were in men with diagnosed low testosterone and do not address use in men with normal levels.

Testosterone products can cause acne, oily skin, swelling and breast enlargement in men, and serious effects reported include liver toxicity, heart disease and stroke, blood clots, raised hematocrit and worsened sleep apnea or benign prostatic hyperplasia.[1] Exogenous testosterone can suppress sperm production, sometimes causing reversible infertility.[1] Women and children exposed to the hormone can develop virilisation, and testosterone is contraindicated in pregnancy.[1]

In February 2025, the FDA changed testosterone product labelling, removing boxed-warning language about adverse cardiovascular outcomes and adding a warning about increased blood pressure.[1] Several registered trials have used ambulatory blood pressure monitoring in men on topical or other testosterone products.[3][4]

Applied gel delivers testosterone through the skin into the circulation. In the 2004 study, mean serum dihydrotestosterone levels and the DHT-to-testosterone ratio slightly increased on treatment.[2] Pharmacokinetic comparisons between AndroGel and the Testim gel formulation have been published.[5] Testosterone is highly protein bound (97 to 99.5 percent) and mainly metabolised in the liver.[1]

Testosterone is a controlled substance in many countries and prescription-only in most, and is banned in sport by the World Anti-Doping Agency.[1] US use of testosterone roughly tripled between 2001 and 2011, and in 2023 it was the 119th most prescribed medication in the United States.[1] A claims analysis studied adherence in men treated with topical testosterone.[6]

A 2004 open study of 163 hypogonadal men using 1 percent gel for up to 42 months reported normalised testosterone and sustained improvements in sexual function, mood, body composition and bone density.[2] A 2003 three-year preliminary report also followed hypogonadal men on gel.[7] A 2010 comparison examined clomiphene citrate versus gel for hypogonadism, including cost.[8] A 2016 study reported that oral enclomiphene raised testosterone and preserved sperm counts in obese hypogonadal men unlike topical testosterone.[9] Registered trials include a type 2 diabetes study in hypogonadal men, a prostate cancer study and blood pressure monitoring studies.[3][4][10]

timeline.event: FDA states benefits and safety for age-related low testosterone not established.[1]
